title: Divisor identities and proof by prime powers
question: When is checking prime powers a proof rather than a shortcut?
summary: Multiplicativity is the bridge from a local prime-power calculation to an identity for every positive integer.
definition: An arithmetic function \(F\) is multiplicative when \(F(1)=1\) and \(F(ab)=F(a)F(b)\) whenever \(\gcd(a,b)=1\). It is completely multiplicative when the product rule holds for all positive \(a,b\).

Write \(\omega(n)\) for the number of distinct prime factors of \(n\), with \(\omega(1)=0\). The Möbius function \(\mu\) is zero on integers divisible by a prime square and equals \((-1)^{\omega(n)}\) on squarefree integers.
Dirichlet convolution is \((F*G)(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}F(d)G(n/d)\). Its identity \(\varepsilon\) equals \(1\) at \(n=1\) and \(0\) otherwise.
theorem: For every positive \(n\), \(\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi(d)=n\) and \(\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(d)^2=2^{\omega(n)}\). If \(f\) is completely multiplicative with \(f(1)=1\), its Dirichlet-convolution inverse is the function \(n\mapsto\mu(n)f(n)\).
proof: First justify reduction to prime powers. If \(F,G\) are multiplicative and \(\gcd(a,b)=1\), every divisor of \(ab\) has a unique form \(d=d_1d_2\) with \(d_1\mid a\) and \(d_2\mid b\). Then \(F(d)=F(d_1)F(d_2)\), while \(G(ab/d)=G(a/d_1)G(b/d_2)\). Summing independently over \(d_1\) and \(d_2\) gives \((F*G)(ab)=(F*G)(a)(F*G)(b)\). Thus convolution preserves multiplicativity. The constant-one function, \(\varphi\), and \(\mu^2\) are multiplicative; so are their stated divisor sums. The functions \(n\mapsto n\) and \(n\mapsto2^{\omega(n)}\) are multiplicative too.

For a prime power \(p^k\), including \(k=0\), \(\sum_{j=0}^{k}\varphi(p^j)=1+\sum_{j=1}^{k}(p^j-p^{j-1})=p^k\). Also \(\mu(p^0)^2=1\), \(\mu(p)^2=1\), and \(\mu(p^j)^2=0\) for \(j\ge2\). Thus the second sum is \(1\) when \(k=0\), and \(2\) when \(k\ge1\), matching \(2^{\omega(p^k)}\). Unique prime factorization and multiplicativity now prove both identities for all \(n\).

For the inverse claim, complete multiplicativity gives \((f*(\mu f))(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}f(d)\mu(n/d)f(n/d)=f(n)\sum_{e\mid n}\mu(e)=f(n)\varepsilon(n)=\varepsilon(n)\). The last equality uses \(f(1)=1\). Convolution is commutative, so this is a two-sided inverse.

example.prompt: Check the squarefree-divisor identity at \(n=18\), then explain why the check is not its general proof.
steps: The positive divisors are \(1,2,3,6,9,18\). The squarefree ones are \(1,2,3,6\), each contributing \(\mu(d)^2=1\); the other two contribute \(0\).
The general argument additionally establishes that both sides are multiplicative and agrees on every prime power.
example.conclusion: Both sides equal \(4\) at \(18\); multiplicativity plus the prime-power calculation proves the theorem.

practice.prompt: The functions \(\tau(n)\) and \(2^{\omega(n)}\) agree at every prime. Does \(\tau(n)=2^{\omega(n)}\) hold for all positive \(n\)?
hints: Count divisors and distinct primes separately.
practice.answer: No. For any prime \(p\), both sides equal \(2\) at \(p\), but \(\tau(p^2)=3\) while \(2^{\omega(p^2)}=2\). Even for multiplicative functions, agreement at primes alone is insufficient; one must check every prime power.

caution: A prime-power computation becomes a general proof only after both sides have been shown multiplicative. Agreement merely at primes is weaker still.

bridge: The inverse calculation uses scalar-valued functions. Over a general coefficient ring, convolution inversion requires \(f(1)\) to be invertible; here it equals \(1\).

title: Perfect numbers and the even classification
question: Why do certain powers of two and Mersenne primes produce perfect numbers?
summary: The sum-of-divisors formula both constructs every even perfect number and forces the same form in the converse.
definition: For a positive integer \(n\), let \(\sigma(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}d\). The integer \(n\) is perfect when its proper positive divisors sum to \(n\), equivalently \(\sigma(n)=2n\).
A Mersenne number has the form \(2^p-1\) for a positive integer \(p\). Calling it prime requires a separate primality test; the shape alone is insufficient.
theorem: An even positive integer is perfect exactly when it has the form \(n=2^{p-1}(2^p-1)\), where \(p\) is a positive integer and \(2^p-1\) is prime. Such a prime forces \(p\) itself to be prime.
proof: Construction: let \(M=2^p-1\) be prime. Since \(M\) is odd and \(\sigma\) is multiplicative, \(\sigma(2^{p-1}M)=(1+2+\cdots+2^{p-1})(1+M)=(2^p-1)2^p=2(2^{p-1}M)\). Thus the displayed even integer is perfect.

Conversely, let \(n\) be even and perfect. Write \(n=2^{k-1}m\) with \(k\ge2\) and odd \(m\). Multiplicativity and perfection give \((2^k-1)\sigma(m)=2^k m\). Since consecutive integers are coprime, \(2^k-1\mid m\); write \(m=(2^k-1)t\) with positive \(t\). The same equation becomes \(\sigma(m)=2^k t=m+t\).

Because \(2^k-1>1\), we have \(t<m\), and both \(1\) and \(t\) divide \(m\). If \(t>1\), then \(1,t,m\) are three distinct positive divisors, giving \(\sigma(m)\ge1+t+m>m+t\), a contradiction. Hence \(t=1\), so \(m=2^k-1\) and \(\sigma(m)=m+1\). An integer greater than \(1\) has divisor sum \(m+1\) exactly when its only positive divisors are \(1,m\); thus \(m\) is prime. Set \(p=k\).

Finally, if \(p=uv\) with integers \(u,v>1\), the factorization \(2^{uv}-1=(2^u-1)(1+2^u+\cdots+2^{u(v-1)})\) has two factors greater than \(1\). Therefore primality of \(2^p-1\) forces \(p\) to be prime.

example.prompt: Check that \(496\) is perfect without listing every divisor individually.
steps: Observe \(496=2^4\cdot31\) and \(31=2^5-1\) is prime: it has no prime divisor at most \(\sqrt{31}<6\): \(2,3,5\) do not divide \(31\).
Since \(992=2\cdot496\), its proper positive divisors sum to \(496\).
example.conclusion: \(496\) is an even perfect number of the classified form.

practice.prompt: Prove that if \(2^r-1\) is prime, then \(r\) is prime. Does prime \(r\) guarantee \(2^r-1\) prime?
practice.answer: If \(r=uv\) with \(u,v>1\), then \(2^u-1\) is a proper divisor greater than \(1\) of \(2^r-1\), so that Mersenne number is composite. The converse fails: \(11\) is prime but \(2^{11}-1=2047=23\cdot89\).

caution: This theorem classifies even perfect numbers. It gives no classification or existence result for odd perfect numbers.

bridge: The proof combines unique factorization with multiplicativity of \(\sigma\); it does not require a conjecture about how often Mersenne primes occur.

title: Floors, fractional parts and counting
question: What exactly is counted by a floor?
summary: Floor separates an integer count from a fractional remainder; its jumps can be read as exact counts of multiples.
definition: For real \(x\), \(\lfloor x\rfloor\) is the greatest integer at most \(x\). Its fractional part is \(\{x\}=x-\lfloor x\rfloor\), always in \([0,1)\), including when \(x<0\).
For integers \(1\le A\le B\) and \(m\ge1\), \(\lfloor B/m\rfloor-\lfloor(A-1)/m\rfloor\) counts multiples of \(m\) in the closed interval \([A,B]\).
theorem: For all real \(x,y\), \(\lfloor x+y\rfloor-\lfloor x\rfloor-\lfloor y\rfloor\) is \(0\) or \(1\), according as \(\{x\}+\{y\}<1\) or \(\ge1\). For any integer \(N\ge1\), the number of positive multiples of \(m\ge1\) at most \(N\) is \(\lfloor N/m\rfloor\).
proof: Write \(x=\lfloor x\rfloor+u\) and \(y=\lfloor y\rfloor+v\), with \(0\le u,v<1\). Then \(\lfloor x+y\rfloor=\lfloor x\rfloor+\lfloor y\rfloor+\lfloor u+v\rfloor\). Since \(0\le u+v<2\), the final floor is exactly \(0\) when the sum is below \(1\), and \(1\) otherwise.

The positive multiples of \(m\) no greater than \(N\) are \(m,2m,\ldots,km\), where \(k\) is the largest integer satisfying \(km\le N\); equivalently \(k=\lfloor N/m\rfloor\). Subtracting the count through \(A-1\) from the count through \(B\) proves the interval formula in the definition.

example.prompt: Compare floor with truncation at \(-7/3\), then count multiples of \(4\) from \(10\) through \(35\).
steps: Because \(-3\le-7/3<-2\), \(\lfloor-7/3\rfloor=-3\), whereas truncation toward zero gives \(-2\). The fractional part is \(\{-7/3\}=-7/3-(-3)=2/3\).
There are \(\lfloor35/4\rfloor=8\) positive multiples through \(35\), and \(\lfloor9/4\rfloor=2\) through \(9\).
example.conclusion: Negative inputs still have fractional part in \([0,1)\), and the interval contains exactly \(6\) multiples of \(4\).

practice.prompt: Count the integers \(k\) with \(20\le k\le95\) and \(6\mid k\). Then find \(\lfloor-5/2\rfloor\) and \(\{-5/2\}\).
hints: Count multiples through \(95\), then subtract those through \(19\).
The floor of a negative noninteger lies below it.

caution: Floor is not linear: the carry from two fractional parts can change the sum by \(1\). Its graph jumps at integers.

bridge: Coprime multiplication permutes the nonzero residue classes, turning a fractional-part sum into an elementary finite sum.

title: Prime exponents in factorials and binomials
question: How often does a prime occur across all factors of a factorial?
summary: Count each prime-power contribution separately. The resulting finite floor sum computes factorial and binomial valuations exactly.
definition: For a prime \(p\) and positive integer \(n\), \(v_p(n)\) is the exponent of \(p\) in \(n\). Define \(n!=1\cdot2\cdots n\), with \(0!=1\).
For integers \(0\le k\le n\), \(\binom nk=n!/[k!(n-k)!]\) is an integer. Valuations of its factorial expression may be subtracted because prime exponents add under multiplication.
theorem: For every prime \(p\) and integer \(n\ge0\), the exponent of \(p\) in \(n!\) is \[v_p(n!)=\sum_{j\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{n}{p^j}\right\rfloor.\] Only finitely many terms are nonzero. For \(0\le k\le n\), subtract the corresponding factorial valuations to obtain the exponent in \(\binom nk\).
proof: Each factor \(m\) in \(n!\) contributes \(v_p(m)\) copies of \(p\). Count the first copy from each multiple of \(p\), a total of \(\lfloor n/p\rfloor\); a second copy from each multiple of \(p^2\), a total of \(\lfloor n/p^2\rfloor\); and so on. Thus \(\sum_{m=1}^{n}v_p(m)=\sum_{j\ge1}\lfloor n/p^j\rfloor\). When \(p^j>n\), the count is zero, proving the sum is finite. The formula also gives \(0\) for \(n=0\), as \(v_p(0!)=v_p(1)=0\).

The identity \(n!=\binom nk k!(n-k)!\) and additivity of \(v_p\) give \[\begin{aligned}v_p\!\left(\binom nk\right)&=v_p(n!)\\&\quad-v_p(k!)\\&\quad-v_p((n-k)!).\end{aligned}\] Substitute the proved factorial formula in each term. At every power \(p^j\), the difference of the three floors is \(0\) or \(1\) by the floor-carry identity applied to \(k/p^j\) and \((n-k)/p^j\). The resulting sum is therefore visibly nonnegative.

steps: For \(p=2\), the floor counts are \(\lfloor15/2\rfloor=7\), \(\lfloor15/4\rfloor=3\), and \(\lfloor15/8\rfloor=1\); higher powers exceed \(15\). Thus \(v_2(15!)=7+3+1=11\).
The multiples of \(4\) contribute a second factor of \(2\), and the multiple \(8\) contributes a third; counting only the seven even factors would miss four copies.

practice.prompt: Compute \(v_3\!\left(\binom{12}{6}\right)\) by the floor formula and independently by evaluating the binomial coefficient.
practice.answer: \(v_3(12!)=\lfloor12/3\rfloor+\lfloor12/9\rfloor=4+1=5\), while \(v_3(6!)=\lfloor6/3\rfloor=2\). Hence \(v_3\!\left(\binom{12}{6}\right)=5-2-2=1\). Independently, \(\binom{12}{6}=924=3\cdot308\), and \(3\nmid308\), so its valuation is \(1\).

caution: Counting only multiples of \(p\) misses the additional copies contributed by multiples of \(p^2,p^3,\ldots\).

bridge: Valuations turn products into sums of prime exponents; the floor formula makes that bookkeeping into exact interval counts.
